title: Erdős Problem #291: Harmonic Number Divisibility
description: Do both gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1 and gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1 occur infinitely often, where H_n = a_n/L_n? Part 2 trivially YES; Part 1 OPEN.

meta.author: Steinerberger, Shiu (2016), Wu-Yan (2022)
originalContributions: L n: LCM of 1 to n
H n: Harmonic number as rational
a n: Numerator when H_n written over L_n
steinerberger_criterion: Leading digit p-1 implies p divides gcd
wolstenholme_theorem: H_{p-1} numerator divisible by p²
meta.assumptions: 2 axioms: wolstenholme_theorem, divisibility_characterization. See Lean source for complete statements.

overview.historicalContext:
The harmonic numbers $H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \cdots + 1/n$ have been studied since antiquity, but their divisibility properties remain mysterious. Writing $H_n = a_n/L_n$ where $L_n = \text{lcm}(1, \ldots, n)$, Erdős asked whether $\gcd(a_n, L_n)$ takes both values 1 and $> 1$ infinitely often.

The key tool is Wolstenholme's theorem (1862): for primes $p \ge 5$, $p^2$ divides the numerator of $H_{p-1}$. This classical result, combined with a characterization linking $p \mid \gcd(a_n, L_n)$ to the leading base-$p$ digit of $n$, makes Part 2 trivial: numbers of the form $(p-1) \cdot p^k$ always have leading digit $p-1$ in base $p$.

Part 1 is far harder. Shiu (2016) gave a heuristic argument predicting $\sim x/\log x$ values of $n \le x$ with $\gcd = 1$, based on treating the divisibility conditions for different primes as approximately independent and applying Mertens' theorem. Wu and Yan (2022) proved conditionally — assuming Schanuel's conjecture (which implies $\mathbb{Q}$-linear independence of $\{1/\log p\}$ for distinct primes $p$) — that the set of $n$ with $\gcd > 1$ has density 1. But even this does not settle Part 1, as a set of density 0 can still be infinite.

Notably, this formalization actually proves Steinerberger's criterion (rather than axiomatizing it), derives Part 2 from it constructively, and provides extensive computational verification including GCD values for $n \le 10$.
overview.problemStatement: Let $L_n = \text{lcm}\{1, \ldots, n\}$ and define $a_n$ by $H_n = a_n/L_n$. Do both $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$ and $\gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1$ occur for infinitely many $n$?
overview.text: Do both gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1 and gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1 occur infinitely often, where H_n = a_n/L_n? Part 2 trivially YES; Part 1 OPEN.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines harmonic numbers as rationals, extracts the numerator $a_n$ when written over $L_n$, and proves the Steinerberger criterion from the divisibility characterization and Wolstenholme's theorem. Part 2 is proved constructively using the infinite family $\{2 \cdot 3^k : k \ge 1\}$ (with an alternate proof via $\{4 \cdot 5^k\}$). Extensive structural properties of $L_n$ and $H_n$ are proved, along with computed GCD values for $n \le 10$.
keyInsights: The divisibility $p \mid \gcd(a_n, L_n)$ depends only on the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$, reducing an analytic question about harmonic sums to a combinatorial one about digit representations. This is the key structural insight enabling the characterization.

Wolstenholme's theorem ($p^2 \mid \text{num}(H_{p-1})$) is much stronger than needed for Part 2 — simple $p$-divisibility suffices. The $p^2$ divisibility connects to Wolstenholme primes (primes where $p^3 \mid \text{num}(H_{p-1})$), of which only 2 are known: 16843 and 2124679.

Part 1 is essentially a problem about correlations between leading digits across different prime bases. The heuristic $\sim x/\log x$ arises from Mertens' third theorem: $\prod_{p \le n}(1 - 1/p) \sim 2e^{-\gamma}/\log n$, treating the digit conditions as independent.

The connection to Schanuel's conjecture is surprising: proving Part 1 unconditionally may require progress on this deep conjecture in transcendence theory, which asserts that $n$ algebraically independent complex numbers have at least $n$ algebraically independent values among their exponentials.

The formalization is unusually computational for an Erdős problem: Steinerberger's criterion is proved (not axiomatized), Part 2 is constructively witnessed, and GCD values are computed via `native_decide` for $n \le 10$, providing a 932-line proof with many verified theorems.

sections.title: Module Header and Overview
sections.summary: File docstring stating Erdős problem 291 (the harmonic-LCM gcd question), references, imports, and namespace/open setup.
sections.mathContext: Erdős 291 asks about gcd(a(n), L(n)) where L(n)=lcm(1,…,n) and a(n) is the integer numerator of H(n)·L(n): Part 1 (infinitely many n with gcd=1) is open; Part 2 (infinitely many with gcd>1) is settled here.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Definitions
sections.summary: Defines L(n)=lcm(1,…,n), H(n)=Σ 1/k as a rational, a(n)=num(H(n)·L(n)), and harmonicGCD(n)=gcd(a(n), L(n)).
sections.mathContext: L is built via Finset.fold Nat.lcm; H is a ℚ-valued harmonic sum; a(n) extracts the natural-number numerator of H(n)·L(n); harmonicGCD is the central object of the problem.

sections.title: Part II: The Problem Statement
sections.summary: Formalizes question_part1 (infinitely many n with gcd=1, OPEN), question_part2 (infinitely many with gcd>1, PROVED), and erdos291Statement as their conjunction.
sections.mathContext: The two parts are stated as Set.Infinite predicates over {n | harmonicGCD n = 1} and {n | harmonicGCD n > 1}; only Part 2 is provable with current techniques.

sections.title: Part III: Leading-Digit Helper (Part 2 is Easy)
sections.summary: Defines leadingDigitAux (fuel-recursive) and leadingDigit n p, the most-significant base-p digit of n — the computational tool behind the Steinerberger criterion.
sections.mathContext: leadingDigit isolates the top base-p digit; the Steinerberger criterion ties the event p ∣ harmonicGCD to this digit equalling p−1, which makes Part 2 tractable via explicit families.

sections.title: Part IV: Wolstenholme's Theorem
sections.summary: States wolstenholme_theorem as an axiom: for primes p ≥ 5, p² divides the numerator of H_{p-1}.
sections.mathContext: Wolstenholme's congruence H_{p-1} ≡ 0 (mod p²) is a classical number-theoretic input; axiomatised here (one of two assumptions) and used to derive the divisibility criterion.

sections.title: Part V: Characterization of Divisibility
sections.summary: States divisibility_characterization as an axiom: p ∣ harmonicGCD(n) iff p divides the numerator of H_k where k is the leading base-p digit of n.
sections.mathContext: This reduces a prime dividing the gcd to a numerator-divisibility test on a single partial harmonic sum indexed by the leading digit; the second axiomatised assumption.

sections.title: Part V.5: Steinerberger's Criterion
sections.summary: Proves steinerberger_criterion: if the leading base-p digit of n is p−1, then p ∣ harmonicGCD(n). Derived from Wolstenholme + the divisibility characterization.
sections.mathContext: Combines wolstenholme_theorem (p² ∣ num H_{p-1}) with divisibility_characterization to conclude p ∣ gcd whenever the leading digit equals p−1 — the engine for constructing gcd>1 families.

sections.title: Part VI: Heuristic and Density
sections.summary: Defines countGCDOne and records Shiu's heuristic: about x/log x values n ≤ x have gcd = 1 (density 0 but infinite), motivating Part 1.
sections.mathContext: The heuristic suggests {n : gcd=1} is infinite yet density-zero, which is exactly why Part 1 resists elementary methods while Part 2 (a positive-density-style event) is reachable.

sections.title: Part VII: Conditional Results
sections.summary: Records the Wu–Yan (2022) conditional result: assuming Schanuel's conjecture, the density of n with gcd > 1 is 1.
sections.mathContext: Conditional density-one for gcd>1 frames Part 1's gcd=1 set as a sparse exceptional set, situating the unconditional Part 2 proof within the known landscape.

sections.title: Part VIII: Why Part 1 is Hard
sections.summary: Explains why Part 1 (infinitely many gcd = 1) is hard: it requires controlling cross-prime correlations of leading-digit events simultaneously.
sections.mathContext: Ruling out p ∣ gcd for all primes p at once amounts to avoiding every 'leading digit = p−1' event, a simultaneous constraint no current technique handles.

sections.title: Part X: Structural Properties of L
sections.summary: Computes L(n) for n ≤ 6 and proves L(n) > 0, L(n) ∣ n!, and k ∣ L(n) for 1 ≤ k ≤ n.
sections.mathContext: Establishes the basic divisibility behaviour of L = lcm(1,…,n): it is positive, divides the factorial, and is divisible by every k in range — used throughout the gcd analysis.

sections.title: Part XII: Structural Properties of H
sections.summary: Computes H(n) for n ≤ 6 and proves the recurrence H(n+1) = H(n) + 1/(n+1), positivity, and strict monotonicity.
sections.mathContext: Pins down the harmonic-number values and order structure (H_succ recurrence, H_pos, H_strict_mono, H_mono) needed to reason about num(H(n)·L(n)).

sections.title: Part XII.5: Small Examples
sections.summary: Proves small_examples (gcd = 1 for n = 1..5, gcd = 3 first at n = 6) and small_gcd_one for 1 ≤ n ≤ 5; first_gcd_gt_one records harmonicGCD 6 = 3.
sections.mathContext: Concrete computed gcd values establish the first occurrence of gcd > 1 at n = 6 (factor 3), anchoring the leading-digit explanation of when primes divide the gcd.

sections.title: Part XIII: Leading Digit Properties
sections.summary: Proves leadingDigit_zero, leadingDigitAux_lt, leadingDigit_lt_base, and concrete leadingDigit evaluations (e.g. ld(2,3)=2, ld(24,5)=4).
sections.mathContext: Foundational facts about the leadingDigit function (boundedness by base, base cases) plus decided concrete values that feed the Steinerberger-criterion applications.

sections.title: Part XIV: GCD Structure
sections.summary: Proves harmonicGCD(n) ∣ L(n), harmonicGCD(n) ∣ a(n), and that any prime dividing harmonicGCD(n) is ≤ n.
sections.mathContext: Structural constraints on the prime factors of the gcd: it divides both a(n) and L(n), and (via prime_dvd_L_le) only primes ≤ n can occur.

sections.title: Part XV: Applying Steinerberger to Concrete Cases
sections.summary: Applies the criterion to concrete cases: 3 ∣ gcd(6), 3 ∣ gcd(8), 5 ∣ gcd(24), and the family lemma 3 ∣ gcd(2·3^k) via leadingDigit_two_times_pow_three.
sections.mathContext: Turns the leading-digit criterion into verified divisibilities, including the parametric leadingDigit(2·3^k,3)=2 computation that seeds the first infinite gcd>1 family.

sections.title: Part XVI: Structural Observations
sections.summary: Proves n ∣ L(n) for n ≥ 1, H(n)·L(n) ≥ 0, and H(n)·L(n) = Σ_{k<n} L(n)/(k+1) (a sum of integers).
sections.mathContext: Auxiliary identities: H(n)·L(n) is a nonnegative integer expressible as Σ L(n)/k, clarifying why a(n) is well-defined and integral.

sections.title: Part XVII: Proving Part 2 (Infinitely Many n with gcd > 1)
sections.summary: Constructively proves part2_trivially_true: the family {2·3^k} gives infinitely many n with 3 ∣ harmonicGCD(n), via an injectivity argument.
sections.mathContext: Set.Infinite is established by injecting ℕ → {n : gcd>1} through k ↦ 2·3^k, each member satisfying 3 ∣ gcd by the Part XV family lemma — the unconditional resolution of Part 2.

sections.title: Part XVIII: Summary
sections.summary: Assembles erdos_291_summary and the headline theorem erdos_291 : question_part2, recording the proved status of Part 2.
sections.mathContext: Top-level statement that Part 2 holds; Part 1 remains open, consistent with the gallery's axiomatized status for this Erdős problem.

sections.title: Part XIX: Generalized Leading Digit for (p-1)·p^k
sections.summary: Proves leadingDigit_pm1_times_pow: the leading base-p digit of (p−1)·p^k is p−1 for p > 1.
sections.mathContext: Generalises the 2·3^k computation to arbitrary base p, giving the leading-digit input needed to build gcd>1 families for every prime p ≥ 3.

sections.title: Part XX: Second Infinite Family via p = 5
sections.summary: Proves 5 ∣ gcd(4·5^k), infinitely_many_five_dvd (the {n : 5 ∣ gcd} set is infinite), and the general prime_dvd_gcd_pm1_pow for primes p ≥ 3.
sections.mathContext: A second independent infinite family {4·5^k} with 5 ∣ gcd, plus the general statement p ∣ gcd((p−1)·p^k) — multiple distinct witnesses for Part 2.

sections.title: Part XXI: Sum of Inverses Modulo p
sections.summary: Verifies Σ k⁻¹ ≡ 0 (mod p) for p = 3,5,7,11,13 and Σ k ≡ 0 (mod p) for p = 3,5,7, all by decide.
sections.mathContext: Decidable modular identities (Wolstenholme-flavoured sums of inverses vanishing mod p) providing the arithmetic backbone for the divisibility evidence.

sections.title: Part XXII: Strengthening Part 2 with Multiple Families
sections.summary: Proves part2_via_five, an alternate proof of question_part2 using the {4·5^k} family.
sections.mathContext: Demonstrates Part 2 via a second prime family, strengthening confidence in the result and illustrating that the construction is not specific to p = 3.

sections.title: Part XXIII: Extended Small Examples
sections.summary: Computes H and L for n = 7..10, proves small_examples_extended, and records gcd values (gcd = 3 at n = 7,8; gcd = 1 at n = 9,10).
sections.mathContext: Extends the computed gcd table into [7,10], confirming the alternation between gcd = 1 and gcd = 3 and supplying further data for the Part 1 evidence.

sections.title: Part XXIV: Concrete Evidence for Part 1
sections.summary: Assembles seven_gcd_one_values: the seven values n ∈ [1,10] with harmonicGCD(n) = 1, as concrete evidence toward the open Part 1.
sections.mathContext: Catalogues the gcd = 1 occurrences in [1,10] as empirical support for the conjecture that infinitely many such n exist (Part 1), which remains unproved.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #291 is OPEN (Part 1) with Part 2 PROVED. The formalization proves Steinerberger's criterion from Wolstenholme's theorem and the divisibility characterization, then constructively demonstrates Part 2 using infinite families $\{(p-1) \cdot p^k\}$. The 932-line Lean proof includes extensive structural theory for $L_n$ and $H_n$, computed GCD values for $n \le 10$, and ZMod verification of sum-of-inverses vanishing.
conclusion.implications: This problem reveals a deep connection between the elementary arithmetic of harmonic numbers and transcendence theory: resolving Part 1 may require understanding the $\mathbb{Q}$-linear independence of $\{1/\log p\}$, which is a consequence of Schanuel's conjecture. The leading-digit characterization reduces an analytic question to combinatorial digit patterns, but the correlations across different prime bases remain intractable.
openQuestions: Are there infinitely many $n$ with $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$? This is Part 1, the main open question. Heuristics predict YES with $\sim x/\log x$ such $n$ up to $x$.
Can the heuristic $\sim x/\log x$ be proved unconditionally, without Schanuel's conjecture? This requires bounding correlations between base-$p$ leading digits for different primes $p$.
What is the distribution of prime factors of $\gcd(a_n, L_n)$? Computed data shows 3 dominates for small $n$, but 5, 7, and larger primes also contribute.
Are there Wolstenholme primes beyond 16843 and 2124679? If a third exists, it would imply $p^3 \mid \gcd(a_{p-1}, L_{p-1})$ for that prime, strengthening the divisibility.
